title: Module 18: Staying Connected When It Matters Most

screens.heading: You are safe here
screens.reassurance: This module will not make any calls or access any of your contacts. You are just reading.
screens.goal: By the end of this module, you will have practical strategies for staying close to family across distances and time zones — and for using technology as a gentle support during difficult times.

screens.heading: The most powerful thing you can do: schedule the call
body: Regular video calls with family do not happen by accident. They happen because someone decided to make them a standing appointment.

Pick a time that works: Sunday afternoons, Wednesday mornings — whatever suits both schedules. Put it in your calendar and protect it like any other appointment. Even 15 minutes of video with a grandchild once a week builds a relationship that phone calls alone cannot.
The first call is the hardest. After that, it becomes the highlight of the week for everyone.
screens.tellMeMore: If grandchildren are involved, involve them in the ritual. Let them pick a show-and-tell item to bring to the call each week. Let them show you something they made. Ask them the same question each time: 'What was the best thing that happened this week?' The structure makes it easy for children and gives everyone something to look forward to.

screens.heading: Navigating time zones
body: If family is scattered across Canada or internationally, time zones require a little planning — but they are easy to manage once you know the reference points.
From Eastern time (Ontario): Vancouver is 3 hours behind. UK is 5 hours ahead in summer. Australia is approximately 14–16 hours ahead.
The quickest way to find the current time anywhere: just ask Siri or Google — 'Hey Siri, what time is it in Vancouver right now?' You will get an instant, accurate answer.
screens.tellMeMore: A shared family calendar (Google Calendar or Apple Family Sharing) is one of the most practical tools for keeping everyone on the same page. Create a calendar called 'Family Calls' and add every scheduled call. Invite family members to the calendar — they see the events in their own time zone automatically. No more time zone confusion or missed calls.

screens.heading: Staying connected after a loss
body: When someone we love dies, or when friends and family move away, technology becomes more important — not less. Video calls let families grieve together even when they cannot be together in person.
A shared photo album is a gentle way to celebrate a life together: everyone adds their favourite memory or photograph of the person who has passed. It becomes a living memorial that grows over time.

Online grief support groups are available through the Canadian Mental Health Association and many hospice organisations — compassionate, moderated communities, available via Zoom, free of charge. Your family doctor or local hospice can provide a referral.
screens.tellMeMore: Grief can also bring isolation — especially for seniors who have lost a spouse or close friend. Online communities for seniors exist specifically to address this: CanadaHelps.org, SeniorCareCanada.ca, and local library-run digital connections programmes all offer ways to meet people and stay socially active without leaving home. Ask your local library what they offer for seniors — many now have weekly digital social hours.

screens.heading: Building your online support network
body: Technology works best when it connects you to real people. Your online support network can include: family on a group chat, friends from a Facebook group or community forum, interest-based groups (gardening, books, faith communities), and local organisations that run virtual programmes.
Many Canadian senior centres now offer virtual programmes — exercise classes, book clubs, crafts — accessible from your device. Call your local senior centre and ask what they offer online.
Connected Canadians (connectedcanadians.ca) offers free one-on-one digital support specifically for older Canadians — by phone, by video, or in person through library partnerships.
screens.tellMeMore: If you are ever feeling isolated, overwhelmed, or just want to talk to someone: Seniors Safety Line in Ontario: 1-866-299-1011, free and confidential. BounceBack Canada (bounceback.ca) offers free phone coaching for mild to moderate depression and anxiety, available in English and French. You do not have to be in crisis to reach out — these services exist precisely for the in-between moments.

screens.heading: Connection is a skill — and technology makes it easier
takeaways: Schedule a regular video call and protect it like an appointment. Even 15 minutes weekly builds strong bonds.
Time zone check: ask Siri — 'What time is it in [city] right now?' Instant and accurate.
After a loss: video calls let families grieve together across distance. Shared photo albums become living memorials.
Canadian Mental Health Association and local hospices offer free Zoom grief support groups.
Connected Canadians offers free one-on-one digital support for older Canadians — by phone, video, or in person.
screens.confidence: You now have the strategies and resources to stay genuinely connected — to family, to community, and to support — no matter the distance or the circumstances.
